source.title: Teaching Models to Balance Resisting and Accepting Persuasion
source.authors: Elias Stengel-Eskin; Peter Hase; Mohit Bansal

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses dialogues generated by smaller models to train larger models and calls this weak-to-strong generalization, but its reported evaluations concern persuasion performance, not whether the student beats its weak supervisor or its PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper trains models with preference data generated from Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B dialogues, including Llama-3.1-70B, and reports downstream persuasion results. It does not report a weak-supervisor score, a strong model trained on true labels, or PGR. The retained rows record selected outcomes of this weak-data-trained 70B model as related findings, not tests of the listed claim versions. Comparisons among PBT, accept-only, and resist-only are the paper's own method comparisons and are not recorded as claim-version rows.
record.test_reason: The paper calls its setup weak-to-strong generalization: dialogues from 7-8B models are used to train Llama-3.1-70B. But the preference labels are scored against TriviaQA reference answers, not weak-model labels. No weak-supervisor score, true-label strong ceiling or PGR is reported. The results show PBT's own gains over the untrained base model, so the paper uses the term without testing any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that PBT, built on dialogue-tree preference data, yields models that resist misinformation and flipflopping while still accepting corrections. PBT also improves and stabilises strong-weak team debate. The authors describe training 70B on 7-8B dialogues as weak-to-strong generalization, but they never compare the 70B student with a weak-label supervisor or a ceiling.
record.recipe_differences: Instead of fine-tuning on weak-model task labels and measuring PGR, the paper constructs dialogue-tree preference pairs from Mistral-7B-v0.2-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B, then performs supervised fine-tuning followed by DPO. It does not compare the student with its supervisor or a true-label ceiling.
record.method_sensitivity: not stated for the weak-to-strong claim; persuasion outcomes vary across PBT, accept-only, and resist-only training.

fits_no_version.finding: Preference data from dialogues between 7-8B models, scored against reference answers, improves Llama-3.1-70B over its untrained base. FARM average misinformation falls from 60.82 to 22.69. Balanced persuasion accuracy rises from 58.01 to 74.56. After-challenge flipflop accuracy rises from 40.10 to 73.40.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ground-truth-scored preference data generated by smaller models can improve a larger model's balance of resisting and accepting persuasion.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2024
record.problems: The study does not evaluate a weak-supervisor baseline, a strong model trained on true labels, or PGR, so its results cannot establish the weak-to-strong comparison in the claim. The authors also note that evaluation is limited to closed-form answers, trivia-like domains, and English.
record.rows_left_out: Other model sizes, accept-only and resist-only conditions, persuasion strategies, and multi-agent team results were not included because they are results of the paper's persuasion method rather than direct measures of weak-to-strong performance or supervisor-relative gap recovery.

untested.parts: No student-vs-weak-supervisor comparison or PGR. Training preferences are scored against ground-truth reference answers, so the supervision is not weak labels.
PBT is compared with accept-only and resist-only training, not with naive weak-label fine-tuning. No PGR is reported.
No analysis of how PGR varies with supervisor or student size, task or representations.
No tests of student exploitation of supervisor blind spots, distribution shift effects on PGR, or shared student-supervisor errors.

record.verdict_notes: The key point is that the preference labels are derived from TriviaQA reference answers through recursive correctness scoring. The smaller models only generate candidate dialogue turns, so the setup is not weak supervision in the sense of the original source. Table 3 does show 70B+PBT (74.56) above 8B and Mistral base (43–45). However, those models are not the label source, so this is not a PGR comparison. Relation could arguably be cites_only, since the paper merely names the phenomenon.

versions.untested_parts: No weak-supervisor comparison, true-label strong ceiling, or PGR is reported.
PBT is compared with accept-only and resist-only training, not with naive fine-tuning using weak labels; no PGR is reported.
The paper trains different model sizes and evaluates multiple persuasion settings, but does not measure how PGR varies with model size, task, or representations.
It evaluates persuasion and team order effects, not student exploitation of supervisor blind spots, PGR under distribution shift, or effects of shared student-supervisor errors.
No theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor are proposed or tested.
